title: The Holy Rosenbergs
wpTitle: Reviews of The Holy Rosenbergs in London starring Tracy-Ann Oberman

ratings.excerpt: Cake, comedy, and a furious row over Gaza … Tracy-Ann Oberman leads a fine cast in the Menier’s revival of Ryan Craig’s sharp play, which explores knotty ethical family dilemmas against the backdrop of war in Israel … ... at the Menier Chocolate Factory, Lindsay Posner’s revival of Ryan Craig’s family drama explores the kind of knotty ethical dilemmas that [Arthur] Miller made his own. … Ryan, though, adds wry humour to the mix. This is an evening where a debate about Israel, the morality of war and the meaning of community can suddenly land a sharp blow to the funny bone. … Time and again, you find yourself laughing through the pain while admiring the finely wrought performances from a cast led by Tracy-Ann Oberman. … Oberman always holds your attention as the indomitable Lesley, the kind

Suburban Jewish family chew over morals and macaroons … Tracy-Ann Oberman stars in this absorbing and timely revival of Ryan Craig’s 2011 comic tragedy, set over one fraught evening … A death in the family is always a reckoning. In this absorbing revival of Ryan Craig’s play from 2011, it is also an unravelling … Craig describes his plays as “comic tragedies … This is a horribly apposite moment for a revival: British Jewry is embattled but painfully conflicted.

Still timely and thought-provoking … Excellent revival of Ryan Craig’s 2011 play about an British-Jewish family in crisis … The Middle East is on fire – again. So Ryan Craig’s brilliantly provocative play, The Holy Rosenbergs, is more relevant than ever. … ... this revival of Craig’s family drama... retains all of its power to disturb. … Craig introduces more layers of complication, Arthur Miller style, examining both the emotional lives of the Rosenbergs and the politics of the Middle East. … If anything, the play is a bit too rich in detail, and the plot twists could be more sharply delivered. Yet there’s a lot to enjoy here: the characterization, especially of the proud yet agitated David, is superb and Craig gives each character plenty of room to express their points of view. … Lindsay

Watching Lindsay Posner’s powerful revival at the Menier Chocolate Factory, slightly tightened and focused but still set in 2009, its resonance... seems almost deafening. … ... the play’s strength is that it grounds its arguments so firmly in a family, bound by tradition and love but separated by politics. … The cast are simply superb … Craig also begins to lean heavily into a discussion of familial guilt that owes too great a debt to Arthur Miller’s All My Sons, and the final confrontation between Ruth and her father doesn’t quite ring true. But Posner and his cast make sure the tension never lessens. … The Holy Rosenbergs is an imperfect play, but a brave and intelligent one too.

Ryan Craig’s 2011 play about a north London Jewish family divided over Israel/Palestine remains grimly topical … ... it’s obvious why director Lindsay Posner might choose to revive The Holy Rosenbergs. … The fact you could make this play today and it would be equally relevant is why it feels more relevant than if it was actually made today. If that makes sense. … Without ever seeming to aggressively both sides it, Craig’s play is compassionate to everyone and, despite some eye watering moments, it seeks to empathise rather than condemn. … There’s a Miller-esque tone to the domestic side of it, with Woodeson’s struggling caterer David having a whiff of Willy Loman to him as he blithely fails to grasp that he’s yesterday’s man. … The trouble is that for all its bracing relevance, the Israel/

A serious but clumsy bid to show how Gaza impacts Jews … This show starring Tracy-Ann Overman at Menier Chocolate Factory brings contemporary moral conundrums into an already-packed drama set in a Jewish family home … Existential troubles pile up on a London Jewish family in Ryan Craig’s depressingly relevant but contrived play from 2011, where the moral conundrums of the Gaza conflict spill and sprawl into a naff Edgware living room. … It’s the concentration of issues rather than the core story that stretches credibility. … And the themes debated – Israel’s right to exist and defend itself, ideas of individual and collective responsibility, the importance of the human stories behind the death tolls – have not changed or softened. … But the way argument is loaded into the play feels forced

Remains thought-provoking … Strong performances hold together this knotty, overstuffed drama about tensions within the Anglo-Jewish community … ... Ryan Craig’s spiky drama about a North London Jewish family torn apart by their divergent politics has only grown more pertinent in the intervening years of intractable conflict and deepening political polarisation. … Though Craig’s writing is contrived... the piece remains thought-provoking.
